title: Undefined Behavior & C's Sharp Edges
relevance: SDE interviews and OAs probe whether candidates grasp that C UB is not just a crash—compilers assume it never happens and can delete safety checks, silently breaking overflow, aliasing, and memory logic under optimization.

phases.goal: Establish the four ISO C behavior categories and that UB means the standard imposes no requirements—not merely an unpredictable crash.

must_hit.point: ISO C buckets program behavior into well-defined, implementation-defined, unspecified, and undefined.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names all four categories and contrasts that well-defined cases (like int x = 5 + 3 yielding 8) have a mandated result.

must_hit.point: Implementation-defined behavior requires the compiler to pick a documented option (e.g. int size may be 16, 32, or 64 bits); unspecified behavior requires a valid choice that need not be documented and may change across compilations (e.g. evaluation order of f(g(), h())).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the int-size and argument-evaluation examples and stresses documentation vs no documentation.

must_hit.point: Undefined Behavior is a state where the C standard imposes absolutely no requirements on the host or compiler; invoking it invalidates the entire program's execution.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Quotes or paraphrases “imposes no requirements” and notes the whole run is invalidated, not just one bad instruction.

must_hit.point: UB does not mean a predictable crash; the compiler may prove UB never happens and aggressively delete safety checks based on that assumption.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts beginner “it just crashes or reads junk” with optimizer freedom to rewrite or delete checks.

probes: What are the four categories of behavior in the C standard, and what does Undefined Behavior actually allow the compiler to do?

hints.1: Start from the ISO buckets—not just “crash vs no crash.”
hints.2: Separate well-defined / implementation-defined / unspecified from UB; then say what “no requirements” implies for optimizers.
hints.3: UB means the standard imposes no requirements; compilers may assume UB never occurs and delete checks that only matter if it did.

phases.goal: Show how common UB sources arise and how compilers turn “X is UB” into axioms that delete checks, prove ranges, and enable optimizations like vectorization.

must_hit.point: In code that dereferences a pointer before a NULL check, NULL dereference is UB, so the compiler may assume the pointer is non-NULL and delete the later safety check.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks the process(int *ptr) pattern: *ptr first, then if (ptr == NULL), and explains the check can be optimized away.

must_hit.point: Signed integer overflow is UB (unlike unsigned wrap), so checks like dist + 100 < dist can be proven false and the whole if deleted to an unconditional success return.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States signed overflow is UB, sketches the check_distance overflow-detection bug, and says the fix is to compare against INT_MAX - 100 before adding.

must_hit.point: Common UB includes out-of-bounds access, use-after-free/double-free/dangling pointers, reading uninitialized locals, strict-aliasing / bad type punning, data races, unsequenced modification (e.g. i = i++), invalid shifts, division by zero and INT_MIN / -1, out-of-bounds pointer arithmetic even without dereference, misaligned access, modifying string literals, and calling through incompatible function pointers.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists several catalog items with a concrete snippet or avoidance rule for each mentioned.

must_hit.point: Compilers treat “X is UB” as an axiom that X is impossible, then use that for optimizations such as Value Range Propagation and Alias Analysis; restrict promises non-overlapping pointers (violating it is UB) and signed loop indices are assumed not to wrap, enabling SIMD vectorization.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions VRP/alias analysis and the restrict dest/src loop example where non-overlap and no signed wrap justify vectorizing.

probes: Why can a NULL check after a dereference, or an overflow check written as dist + 100 < dist, disappear under a modern optimizing compiler?

hints.1: Ask what the compiler is allowed to assume once any earlier operation would be UB.
hints.2: Tie the assumption “UB never happens” to deleting branches that are only useful if overflow or NULL occurred.
hints.3: Dereference-before-check implies ptr cannot be NULL; signed overflow is UB so dist + 100 < dist is assumed false and the if can become unconditional return 1.

phases.goal: Explain why C leaves sharp edges as UB or implementation-defined rather than mandating traps or weaker optimization.

must_hit.point: C targets OS and embedded work where boundary checks cost CPU cycles and the programmer is assumed infallible; mandating predictable runtime trapping like Java or Python was rejected.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the speed/hardware rationale and names trapping languages as the rejected alternative.

must_hit.point: Aggressive exploitation of UB buys extreme execution speed; the rejected alternative is disabling those optimizations so explicit bounds checks survive.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Frames speed vs preserving programmer checks, and notes the compiler is optimizing under algebraic rules—not being “malicious.”

must_hit.point: Implementation-defined and unspecified behaviors hurt portability but do not invalidate the program the way UB does; portable discipline uses fixed-width <stdint.h> types, sizeof instead of hardcoded padding, and unsigned types for bitwise work.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts portability pain vs UB invalidation and lists stdint/sizeof/unsigned practices from the file.

probes: Why does C leave signed overflow and similar cases undefined instead of requiring traps or fully specified wrap, and how does that differ from implementation-defined behavior?

hints.1: Think about where C was meant to run and what checking would cost.
hints.2: Contrast “no requirements / program invalidated” with “documented or undocumented but still valid choices.”
hints.3: OS/embedded speed and infallible-programmer assumption vs Java/Python traps; implementation-defined (e.g. int size) only affects portability, while UB lets optimizers assume the bad case never happens.

phases.goal: Apply tooling and safe idioms: catch UB with sanitizers and analysis, and write checks and type punning that survive optimization.

must_hit.point: Catch UB with UBSan and ASan (-fsanitize=undefined / address), Valgrind for use-after-free and leaks without rebuild, -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic, and static analyzers like clang-tidy and cppcheck; use assert and safe limit computation defensively.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names sanitizers as the strongest everyday tool and mentions Valgrind, warnings, and static analysis from the catching-UB list.

must_hit.point: Prevent signed overflow by checking limits before arithmetic (e.g. dist > INT_MAX - 100), not by testing after an overflowing add.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows or describes the INT_MAX - 100 pre-check fix for check_distance.

must_hit.point: Do not type-pun a float via pointer cast to an integer type (strict aliasing); copy bytes with memcpy or use a union (valid in C99 and later)—compilers optimize memcpy to a register move.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects *(uint32_t *)&f style casts and states memcpy or union as the safe approach.

must_hit.point: Code that appears fine for years at -O0 can break under a modern compiler at -O3 because UB can look like working output until optimization assumptions change.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Connects the “works on my machine” / test-suite trust problem to changing optimization levels.

probes: How do you safely check for signed overflow before it happens, and how do you safely read a float’s raw bits as an integer in C?

hints.1: Avoid performing the risky operation first, then testing the result.
hints.2: For overflow, compare against a limit derived without overflowing; for bits, avoid pointer casts that break aliasing.
hints.3: Use dist > INT_MAX - 100 before adding; use memcpy (or a C99+ union) instead of casting float* to uint32_t*.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: C chose no mandated traps so OS and embedded code avoid paying for boundary checks every time; the programmer is assumed correct, and in exchange the compiler may assume UB never occurs and optimize aggressively.

tradeoffs.topic: Aggressive UB-based optimization vs preserving explicit bounds checks
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Exploiting UB (VRP, alias analysis, restrict, no signed wrap) enables extreme speed such as SIMD vectorization; turning those opts off would keep more of the programmer’s checks but forgoes that performance—the compiler is applying algebraic rules, not acting maliciously.

Unsigned overflow wraps predictably; signed overflow is UB because hardware representations differed historically, so portable code must check limits before signed arithmetic rather than detecting wrap after the fact.

UB invalidates the whole program and licenses any transformation; implementation-defined and unspecified only threaten portability (int size, char signedness, padding, right-shift of negatives)—discipline is fixed-width types, sizeof, and unsigned for bitwise ops, not assuming those details.

gotchas.trap: Treating UB as “unpredictable memory” because out-of-bounds access happened to print a nearby variable on one machine.
gotchas.correction: UB means the compiler may unravel program logic under the assumption you never wrote UB—not merely that you read junk bytes.

gotchas.trap: Believing the compiler is malicious when it deletes a safety check.
gotchas.correction: The compiler only knows the algebraic rules of the abstract machine; deleting a branch it proved impossible is an attempt to make valid programs faster.

gotchas.trap: Writing safety checks after an operation that already could be UB (NULL deref, overflowing add).
gotchas.correction: Validate pointers before use and check limits before arithmetic; once UB is invoked, later checks may be assumed unreachable and removed.

gotchas.trap: Trusting a test suite that only checks outputs, or code that “worked for years” at -O0.
gotchas.correction: UB can silently look correct until compiler version or -O3 changes assumptions; use sanitizers, warnings, and static analysis—not output-only tests.

gotchas.trap: Detecting overflow with if (dist + 100 < dist) or type-punning with *(int*)&f / *(uint32_t *)&f.
gotchas.correction: Those patterns are themselves UB (signed overflow / strict aliasing); use pre-checks against INT_MAX - 100 and memcpy or a union for bit reinterpretation.
